newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tax bill debate centered on fairness issue.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tax bill debate centered on fairness issue.

text.p: The tug-of-war over tax legislation continued Wednesday on Capitol Hill as Democrats and Republicans wrangled over whose plan was the fairest of them all.

"With respect to fairness, I don't think there is any question that the president's proposal fairly allocates benefits of tax cuts to working families," Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said after briefing House Democrats on President Clinton's tax cut proposal.

Democratic lawmakers and aides who attended the meeting said Rubin told them Clinton would veto any tax legislation that included "indexing" which takes into account the effects of inflation and so reduces the taxable amount. Rubin later told Reuters he had not used the "veto" word in the briefing.
The House tax bill includes indexing and would take into account inflation when calculating the capital gains tax on profits made from investments such as stocks.
House and Senate lawmakers will start meeting Friday to work out differences in their respective tax bills with the goal of voting on one compromise bill before the August recess.
The chairman of the House tax-writing committee said 76 percent of the tax relief in the House tax bill would go to people who make less than $75,000.
Democrats say the Republican tax plans give too large a share of the tax cuts to the wealthy.
House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, said the Treasury Department's definitions artificially inflated incomes.
"Q. When does a married couple ... who each make $27,000 become $93,000 earners? A. When the Department of the Treasury figures their income," a statement from Archer said.

The Clinton administration wants the proposed $500 per child tax credit to be available to more low-income families who would be excluded under the Republican legislation because they do not owe enough tax. Republicans argue Democrat tax plans structure the child credit so that families who are not paying taxes would receive money from the government and have likened that to "welfare".
"The GOP tax plan delivers tax relief to people who pay taxes and that's the bottom line," Archer said.

Republicans want to tone down part of the aviation tax provisions in the House and Senate bills. Archer said the $15.50 international arrival and departure fee in the House bill was too high and he preferred it be lowered to the initial $10 fee proposal. Currently there is a $6 departure fee.

Assistant Senate Majority Leader Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican, said earlier this week he expected a proposed 10 percent tax on domestic legs of international flights in the Senate bill would not be included in the final tax bill.

Meanwhile, Democratic House and Senate leaders said they wanted the final tax bill to extend the ethanol subsidy program through 2007. The House tax bill would end the ethanol subsidy after it expired at the end of 2000, while the Senate would keep the subsidy but lower it in later years.

The tax legislation would implement the tax portion of a budget agreement reached between congressional leaders and the White House in May calling for eliminating the deficit over five years and giving $85 billion in net tax cuts.

However, unexpectedly strong tax revenues going into Treasury have reduced the deficit faster than expected with Wall Street analysts expecting the deficit to be about $50 billion by the end of the current fiscal year, from a $107 billion deficit in fiscal 1996.

House Majority Leader Dick Armey, a Texas Republican, saw that as an opportunity for another tax cut bill next year. "It's only right that we return that windfall to hardworking Americans with another tax cut next year," he said.
